1A  Vocabulary
Description
Students play a bingo style game to practise numbers 0–10
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 3d, page 5
Time
10 minutes
Extra material None
Instructions
a Draw a grid with nine squares on the board:
b Ask SS to call out numbers at random from 0–10.
Fill the numbers in at random on the grid.
10
2
6
0
3
c Divide SS into pairs. Ask them to copy the grid
into their notebooks, but to write their numbers
in a different order.
d Call out numbers at random. SS listen and circle
the numbers as they hear them. The first pair to
get three numbers in a row (horizontal, vertical, or
diagonal) wins a point.

1B  Grammar
Description
Students correct errors in six short dialogues to practise language from the lesson
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 4d, page 7
Time
15 minutes
Extra material Print out, photocopy, and cut in half a Where are you from? worksheet – one for each student
Instructions
a Write on the board:
Where he from?

Ask SS to find the error. Get a volunteer to come
to the board to correct the sentence (‘Where’s
he from?’). Explain that it’s good to be able to
recognize written errors. This can help improve
accuracy.
b Divide SS into pairs. Give each student a copy of
the worksheet ‘Where are you from?’ Ask SS to
work together to find and correct the dialogues.
c When pairs have finished ask them to compare
answers with another pair. Review any answers
SS disagree about with the class.
Answers
1 A Where’s Keira Knightley from?

B I think she’s from Ireland.

C No, she isn’t. She’s English.
2 A Is it from Mexico?

B No, it isn’t. It’s from Brazil.
3 A I’m Hiro. I live in Hong Kong, China.

B Are you Chinese?

A No, I’m not. I’m Japanese.
4 A Where are you from?

B I’m from Hungary.

A Is she from Hungary too?

B No, she isn’t. She’s from Spain.
5 A Are you from Russia?

B Yes, I am. Where are you and Aslan from?

A We’re from Turkey.
6 A Where are they from?

B They’re from Russia.

A Where in Russia?

B St Petersburg.

1C  Listening and grammar
Description
Students listen to a text and complete the gaps
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 5, page 9
Time
20 minutes
Extra material Print out, photocopy and cut up the I’m from Japan worksheet – one half for each pair of students
Instructions
a Divide SS into pairs, As and Bs. Give a copy of
worksheet A to all the As and B to the Bs. Tell SS
not to look at each other’s worksheets.
b Explain to SS that they have to read their text to
their partner, who listens and completes the gaps.
A starts reading Text 1 to B. When A has finished,
B reads Text 2 to A.
c When pairs have finished, encourage them to
read each other’s texts, and peer correct.
activities: read each other’s texts, and peer correct.

2A  Vocabulary
Description
Students practise classroom language
Lesson link
Use this activity before students open their books to start the lesson
Time
10 minutes
Extra material None
Instructions
a Tell SS that you are going to give some
instructions and they must do what you say. The
instructions will either be for the whole class, e.g.
‘Stand up, please’, or for individual SS only, e.g.
‘Jaime and Sara, please stand up.’
b Give out some instructions, such as

Close your books.
_______, close the door.
Open your books.
_______, open the door.
Look at the board, please.
Look at your books.
_______, look at _______.
etc.
c After a few minutes you could ask a student to
take over your role, or you could divide the class
into groups and get each group to choose ‘an
instructor’.
activities: Look at the board, please.
Look at your books.

2B  Grammar and vocabulary
Description
Students discuss personal possessions and practise using possessive adjectives; possessive s
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 1c, page 16
Time
10 minutes
Extra material A small bag for each group or one bag for the class
Instructions
a Divide SS into groups of three or four. Give each
group a bag (or pass one bag around the class).
Ask SS to secretly put one of their possessions in
it.
b Gather in the bag(s). Pick up a possession from
one of the SS’ desks, e.g. a pen. Say ‘This is
_____’s pen.’ Write it on the board. Elicit ‘Is this
____’s pen?’ ‘Yes, it is. / No, it isn’t.’ Do some brief
fluency drills.
c Give out one bag of possessions to each group
or ask each student to take one object from the
bag. Explain that SS have two minutes to look
at the possession and decide who each object
belongs to. Tell SS to refer to the language on the
board. (Higher level SS could give a reason for
their answer, e.g. ‘I think it’s Pietro’s MP3 player
because he likes music.’)
d After two minutes ask some SS to ask across the
classroom to see if they have guessed correctly.
For example, ‘Elena, is this your mobile phone?’
‘Yes, it is.’ / ‘No, it isn’t.’
e Write any useful vocabulary, phrases, or
corrections on the board for the class to copy.

2C  Speaking
Description
Students play a memory game using adjectives
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 2c, page 18
Time
15 minutes
Extra material Print out, photocopy, and cut up the Adjectives worksheet – one for each group
Instructions
a Divide SS into groups of three or four.
b Tell them that they are going to play a game with
adjectives. Explain that all the pieces of paper
have one adjective on them and that SS should
put them face down on the table/desk so that
they can’t see the words. The aim is to match
opposites, e.g. if a student picks up old, he also
needs to pick up new to win.
c Each student takes it in turn to pick up two pieces
of paper. If they are opposites, the student keeps
the two pieces of paper and plays again. If they
aren’t opposites, the student must put them back
face down. Everyone in the group must be able to
see the pieces of paper.
d The winner is the person with the most pairs at
the end. Get feedback from class to check all pairs
are correct.

3B  Speaking
Description
Students play a game to review food vocabulary
Lesson link
Use this activity at the end of the lesson
Time
10 minutes
Extra material None
Instructions
a Tell SS that you are going to play a game to
review food vocabulary.
b Divide SS into pairs / groups of three and ask
them to choose a team name. Write the team
names on the board so that you can keep scores.
Tell SS that you are going to call out three letters
in a row. SS must write the letters down and
think of a food word that begins with each one,
e.g. You call out ‘A, B, C’, SS could write apple,
banana, chocolate. ‘E, F, H’ could be eggs, fish,
hamburger. The first team to get three words
scores a point (it’s OK to award points for any
extra food vocabulary that SS might know even
if it hasn’t been taught in the lesson). If SS do
produce new vocabulary, take a note of this, and
review it with the class at the end of the lesson.

Suggestions for letters to call out:

TCS (e.g. tea, cheese, sugar/salad/sandwich)

SMP (e.g. sugar/salad/sandwich, meat/milk,
potatoes/pasta)

OPS (e.g. orange juice, potatoes/pasta, sugar/
salad/sandwich)

TVW (e.g. tea, vegetables, wine)

FBM (e.g. fruit, bread/butter, meat/milk)

And any other combinations.

3C Grammar and pronunciation
Description
Students read two short texts to review present simple: he, she, it and 3rd person s endings
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 5b or 6d, page 29
Time
15 minutes
Extra material Print out, photocopy and cut up a My dream job worksheet – one for each student
Instructions
a Divide SS into pairs. Write on the board: ‘What’s
your dream job?’ Give SS two minutes to ask and
answer the question. After they have finished, ask
them to feed back some of their ideas. Write any
useful vocabulary on the board for the class to
copy.
b Give each student a copy of the worksheet My
dream job. Ask them to skim read the text and tell
you the general theme.
c Pre-teach / elicit the meaning of youth hostel,
interpreter, and translate. Explain / elicit what
‘refer to’ means in the first question. Do an
example with the class – Line 1, text 1: ‘What
does ‘he’ refer to?’ Elicit ‘Johan’. Explain that
knowing who or what pronouns refer to can help
SS understand a text.
d Divide SS into pairs and tell them to work through
question 1 on the worksheet together.
e Review the answers to question 1 with the class.
f Draw SS’ attention to question 2 on the
worksheet. Ask them to find a verb in Line 1,
text 1 (is). Say ‘What sound does the s ending
have?’ Elicit /z/. Ask SS to work through question
2 together. Encourage them to talk about their
answers and practise the pronunciation of the 3rd
person s endings.
Answers

Johan is /z/ Swiss, but he works /s/ in a youth
hostel in Australia. He answers /z/ the telephone
and takes /s/ room reservations. He also
welcomes /z/ the guests when they arrive.
Johan says /z/, ‘Guests from all over the world
stay here and English is the common language
of communication. I really enjoy meeting people
and using English every day.’

Nina works /s/ as an interpreter for a TV news
station. She speaks /s/ seven languages and she
uses /Iz/ English most of all. She uses /Iz/ it with
journalists and also when she speaks /s/ on the
phone. She also watches /Iz/ news reports and
translates /s/ them into other languages. Nina
says /z/, ‘I love my job. I travel and meet people
from around the world. It’s great!’
1 he = Johan; they = the guests; she = Nina;
it = English; it = her job
2 See text above
3 (Students’ own answers)

4A  Vocabulary
Description Students read a text and correct errors with collocations
Lesson link Use this activity after exercise 5d, page 35
Time
15 minutes
Extra material Print out and photocopy the My Typical Day worksheet – one for each student (Use worksheet 1 for weaker SS and
worksheet 2 for stronger SS).
Instructions
a Ask SS if they can think of any people who might
have a different daily routine. Elicit doctor, nurse
(working a night shift), and any more SS might
know. Elicit DJ. Ask SS what they think a DJ’s
typical day might be like.
b Divide SS into pairs. Give each student a copy of
the worksheet My Typical Day. Pre-teach / elicit
club, fashionable, and equipment. Explain that
they should read the text and correct the errors.
These are the bold phrases in text 1.
c After SS have finished the exercise, join two pairs
together and ask them to compare their answers.
Review any answers that the class disagrees
about.
Answers

My name is Jaden and I’m a DJ at a popular
club in Ibiza, Spain. My day is quite different
from most people’s. I [get up] at about 2.00
p.m. in the afternoon. I [have lunch] – usually
just a coffee and a sandwich. After lunch I [do
some housework] and then go for a walk. I
often [go shopping]. I buy a lot of T-shirts and
trainers – I have to look fashionable in the club.
At 6.00 p.m. I [go to the gym] for about an
hour. I usually invite friends to my house in the
evening. I love cooking, so I [make dinner]
and we all eat together. At 9.30 p.m. I go to
the club. I [go to work] in a big car, because
I have to take all my equipment and my music
collection. I DJ until about 4.00 in the morning.
After work I [have breakfast] at the club and
then I [go home]. At about 5.00 in the morning
I [go to bed], just before most people [get
up]!

Description
Students write about a town or city
Lesson link
Use this activity at the end of the lesson
Time
20 minutes
Extra material None
Instructions
a Ask SS to think about the Hammerfest text.
b Write on the board:
Why does the writer use a lot of statistics?
Who would read this type of text?

Explain / elicit the meaning of statistics. Divide SS
into pairs. And give them three minutes to discuss
the questions. While SS are talking write on the
board:
What’s the city / town called?
Where is it?
How many people live there?
Do a lot of tourists visit?
What do people do there?

Check answers to the first two questions.
(Answers: to make the text more interesting;
tourists)
c Divide SS into pairs / groups of three and ask
them to nominate a writer. Tell them to think
about a city anywhere in the world. Ask them to
write approximately 25 – 50 words about the city.
Refer them to the questions on the board and
suggest that they use these as a plan to structure
their writing. Explain that it is the process of
writing – thinking carefully about vocabulary and
grammar that is important in this exercise so SS
should work as a group and discuss their ideas.
Set SS about 15 minutes to write.
d When the texts are finished, stick them on the
wall for other groups to read.

activities: a Ask SS to think about the Hammerfest text.

4C  Speaking
Description
Students discuss rules and laws around the world
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 3d, page 39
Time
15 minutes
Extra material Print out and photocopy the Rules around the world worksheet – one for each pair of students
Instructions
a Ask SS if they know any interesting or strange
rules or laws in other countries. Discuss some
examples briefly if SS know some.
b Divide SS into pairs and hand out a copy of
worksheet Rules around the world.
c Set a time limit of ten minutes. Ask SS to discuss
the questions on the worksheet. Encourage them
to expand their answers as much as possible.
After ten minutes ask the class to report some of
their ideas. Write useful vocabulary and phrases
on the board for SS to copy.
Answers

You can drive in New Zealand when you’re 14.
(False; it is 15 when after passing a test you can
only drive alone between 6.00 a.m. and 10.00
p.m. You can get a full licence at 17.)

You can get married at 16 in Scotland. (True)

In Australia a child can’t buy cigarettes, but can
smoke. (True)

You can’t skateboard in a police station in
Miami, Florida. (True)

You can drink alcohol at 18 in the UK. (True)

In France you can’t name a pig Napoleon.
(True)

You can’t eat chewing-gum in Singapore. (True)

In Switzerland you can’t wash your car on
Sunday. (True)

5A  Writing
Description
Students write about a famous person’s history and practise past simple: be and in, on, at
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 3d, page 45
Time
20 minutes
Extra material None
Instructions
a Divide SS into pairs / groups of three and ask
them to nominate a writer. Ask them to choose
a famous person (preferably whose history they
don’t really know). Tell SS that they’re going to
write an imaginary history for their chosen person.
Ask ‘What information should you write about
your famous person?’, ‘Which grammar should
you use?’ (Elicit past simple be). Write some of
their suggestions on the board. Make sure they
include:
the name they had before they were famous
where they lived
what their house was like
what their job was
where they worked
what kind of car they had
b Set a time limit of ten minutes and tell groups to
write approximately 30–50 words. Explain that it
is the process of writing that is important and that

Instructions

My favourite room is…
There is / are…

Tell SS to think of a room that they like. It could
be a room in their home, or in a hotel they’ve
stayed in, or a room they remember from their
childhood. (It could even be an imaginary room.)
b Ask SS to copy the sentence prompts into their

6C  Grammar
Description
Students read a text to review object pronouns
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 3c, page 59
Time
20 minutes
Extra material Print out and photocopy the It’s a small world! worksheet – one for each student
Instructions
a Hand out a copy of the worksheet ‘It’s a small
world!’ to each student. Pre-teach / translate the
meaning of coincidence. Ask SS to skim read the
text to get an idea of what it’s about (set a time
limit of 30 seconds for this). After the 30 seconds
ask SS some quick comprehension questions, e.g.
Where do the people meet? (at the airport), etc.
b Draw SS’ attention to the gaps in the text. Ask
which word might go in the first gap. Elicit us and
ask SS what kind of word it is (object pronoun).
Ask SS what us refers to, elicit the writer and the
writer’s boyfriend (‘my boyfriend and I’ in the
text). Ask SS to draw a circle around ‘my boyfriend
and I’ and join it to us with a line.
c Set a time limit of ten minutes. Ask SS to read
the text again in detail and answer the questions
on the worksheet. Suggest that SS work together
in pairs or small groups, and encourage them to
discuss their answers.
d After the time limit review the questions with the
class.
Answers

It’s a small world!

Five years ago my boyfriend and I went to Japan
to teach English. As we waited at the airport a
young man sat down next to us. We started
talking to him. He said his name was Peter
Mason. He asked what we studied at university.
‘English Literature,’ said my boyfriend. ‘Music,’ I
said.

‘Me too,’ he replied. ‘I studied music in
Salamanca in Spain. I finished my course last
month.’

‘Really?’ I said, ‘My friend Lorna studied music in
Salamanca.’

He looked surprised, ‘Lorna? Do you mean
Lorna Murray?’

‘Yes!’ I said.

‘I know her really well. We were flat mates!’ said
Peter.

We were amazed – it was such a coincidence!
We talked for the rest of the flight. When we got
to Japan we exchanged mobile phone numbers.
Peter said, ‘My girlfriend’s flying here tomorrow.
We should meet and walk around Osaka
together.’

A few days later he phoned, ‘Come and meet
me and my girlfriend Maria.’ We met them in
Osaka and had a great time.

Later I phoned my friend Lorna. ‘I met your
friend Peter Mason on the plane to Japan.’
‘Wow’, she said. ‘It’s a small world!’
2 us = my boyfriend and I; him = a young man;
Me = Peter; you = the writer;

her = Lorna Murray; it = the coincidence; them
= Peter and his girlfriend;

it = the world
3 It’s not important to identify all the examples
here. Just elicit some answers from the
students. (we = us; you = you; he = his; she =
her; it = it; they = them)
4 Students’ own answers.
activities: ask SS some quick comprehension questions, e.g.
ask SS what kind of word it is (object pronoun).
Ask SS what us refers to, elicit the writer and the
discuss their answers.

7C  Vocabulary
Description
Students do a miming game to review verb collocations
Lesson link
Use this activity after exercise 4c, page 69
Time
10–20 minutes
Extra material A small bag and a copy of the worksheet Verb collocations (cut up and put in the bag)
Instructions
a Before class, cut up one copy of the worksheet
Verb collocations where indicated. Fold each
piece of paper in half and put them into a small
bag.
b Ask SS to close their books. Elicit verbs from the
collocations in exercise 4a and write them on the
board.
c Divide the class into teams of two or three. Tell
SS that they’re going to have a competition to see
which team can guess the most collocations. Ask
SS to pick a team name. Write each name along
the top of the board to keep track of their scores.
d Show the class the bag with the collocations in it.
e Teams take turns to come to the front of the
class and pick two collocations out of the bag. SS
then mime the collocations for the other teams
to guess. Ask SS to put up their hands rather
than shout out and only award a point for a
grammatically correct answer. The team with the
most correct guesses wins.
